h1: Average Cost to Tear Off and Replace a Roof (2026 Guide for Newark, NJ Homes)
leadPhrase: average cost to tear off and replace roof

runs.v: The average cost to tear off and replace a roof in 2026 ranges from $8,000 to $25,000 across the United States, with most homeowners landing between $12,000 and $16,000 for a typical asphalt shingle project. In Newark and Essex County, where labor rates run higher than national figures and older housing stock adds complexity, the average cost to tear off and replace a roof on a 1,700 to 2,000 square foot home falls between $11,000 and $25,000 for architectural asphalt shingles. Complete roof replacements generally run between $4.00 and $15.00+ per square foot, depending on material choice and roof complexity.

This article covers full tear-off and replacement of residential roofs, not minor roof repairs, not overlays, and not DIY projects. The numbers and examples focus on Newark and Essex County homes in 2026, though national benchmarks are included for comparison. If you manage a commercial flat roof, costs follow a different structure; we touch on flat systems briefly, but the core of this guide targets single-family and small multifamily residential properties. The readers who will get the most from this guide are Newark and Essex County homeowners, landlords, and property managers planning a roof replacement project in the next 6 to 18 months.
Here is what you will walk away with:

sections.heading: Understanding Roof Tear-Off and Replacement Costs

runs.v: A full tear-off and replacement means stripping the entire roof down to bare decking, inspecting the roof structure for damage, and installing a complete new roofing system from scratch. That system includes synthetic underlayment, ice and water shield at eaves and valleys, drip edge, step and counter flashing, ridge vents or other ventilation, new shingles or other roofing material, and final cleanup with debris hauling. This is the standard scope for
and across New Jersey.

This differs from an overlay (also called a re-roof), where new shingles are nailed directly over old shingles without removing the existing roofing material. New Jersey's Uniform Construction Code limits roofs to two layers of asphalt shingles, and many manufacturer warranties require installation on a clean deck. Because of these code and warranty requirements, plus the freeze-thaw cycles common in North Jersey, full tear-off is the standard approach for most roofs in this area. Every cost figure in this article assumes a complete tear-off unless stated otherwise.
What "Tear-Off" Includes

Tear-off means removing all existing layers of shingles, underlayment, and nails from the roof deck. Crews also strip damaged flashing, pull old vents, and haul all debris into a dumpster for disposal. Removing old roofing materials costs between $0.40 and $2.00 per square foot, depending on material type and number of layers. For a single layer of asphalt shingles, most Newark contractors charge $1.00 to $2.00 per square foot for tear-off, which covers labor, dumpster rental, and disposal costs at local landfills where Class B tipping fees run $85 to $125 per ton.

Several factors push tear-off costs higher. Removing multiple layers of old roofing increases labor and disposal costs; stripping two or three layers typically adds 60% to 75% to the base tear-off price. Heavy materials like slate or clay tiles take longer to remove and weigh more, increasing both labor time and disposal fees. Steep pitch (above 7/12) requires harnesses and scaffolding, adding roughly 15% to 30% to tear-off costs compared to a walkable slope. Tight lot access, which is common on Newark row homes in the Ironbound and Central Ward, can complicate dumpster placement and slow debris removal.

At Newark Quality Roofing, tear-off crews place protective tarps over landscaping, siding, and walkways before work begins. On row homes and properties with shared walls, we coordinate with neighbors and take extra precautions to protect adjacent structures during the entire process.
What "Replacement" Covers

The replacement phase begins once the old roof is stripped and the deck is inspected. New underlayment goes down first, followed by ice and water shield along eaves and valleys (required in New Jersey's climate zone), drip edge along all roof edges, and step flashing at walls and chimneys. Vents, pipe boots, and ridge ventilation are installed next, and then the new shingles or other roofing system goes on. The project wraps with a final cleanup and a magnet sweep of the yard and driveway to catch stray nails.

For architectural asphalt shingles in the Newark area, the installed cost (materials plus labor, excluding tear-off) typically runs $4.50 to $9.00 per square foot in 2026. Roofing materials alone can cost between $3 and $8 per square foot before labor. Additional components like flashing and ventilation can add to total roofing costs beyond the base shingle price. When you see "average cost to tear off and replace roof" figures in this article, they always refer to the complete system, from tear-off through final inspection, not just the shingles.
Once you understand what is included, the next step is looking at the actual dollar ranges you can expect to see on a quote.

sections.heading: How Much Does It Cost to Tear Off and Replace a Roof in 2026?

runs.v: With the scope defined, here are the 2026 pricing benchmarks for Newark and Essex County. The examples below use asphalt shingles as the baseline because they are the most common roofing material in the area. Other materials shift the range; those comparisons follow in a later section.
National and Newark-Area Averages

Across the U.S., a full tear-off and replacement for asphalt shingle roofs on modest-size homes costs $9,000 to $30,000+, with the national average for a typical asphalt roof often around $12,000 to $16,000. The average cost to replace a roof, considering all material types and larger homes, is around $30,680.

Newark and Essex County run above many national benchmarks. According to local cost models, a typical single-family home in Essex County with architectural asphalt shingles and a full tear-off falls between $11,500 and $17,000 for mid-complexity roofs, with steeper or more complex projects reaching $25,000 and above. Several factors specific to North Jersey explain the higher cost: labor rates in Essex County exceed the national median (NJ crews charge $68 to $110 per hour versus lower rates in many states), older two- and three-story homes require more safety equipment and time, and building code requirements for underlayment and ventilation add material costs that simpler climate zones do not require.
For commercial flat roofs, costs follow a different pricing model. Flat systems like TPO, EPDM, and
are priced differently per square foot due to membrane material costs, insulation layers, and edge detailing. Those numbers appear in the material comparison section below.
Cost Per Square Foot and Per Roofing Square

Roof replacement pricing is often based on the square footage of the roof, not the floor area of the home. A roofing square equals 100 square feet of roof surface. Contractors use this unit because it standardizes pricing across different roof sizes.

For full tear-off and replacement with standard architectural asphalt shingles in the Newark area, 2026 costs run approximately $4.50 to $8.50 per square foot installed. On a per-square basis, that translates to $450 to $850 per roofing square. Local cost models use a rate of about $6.25 per square foot for an average Newark roof of 1,824 square feet, arriving at approximately $11,400 for a full asphalt shingle replacement.

Here is a worked example: an 1,800 square foot roof (actual roof surface area, including pitch factor) at $6.50 per square foot comes to $11,700. Add $400 to $800 for permits and inspections, $500 for contingency on minor deck repairs, and the total project cost reaches roughly $12,600 to $13,000. Steeper roofs, multiple dormers, or premium materials push that number higher.
Those ranges are broad because several key factors can push your quote up or down.

sections.heading: Key Factors That Affect the Average Cost to Tear Off and Replace a Roof

runs.v: Roof size directly affects the total replacement cost, but material choice, roof complexity, local labor rates, and the condition of your existing roof all play a role. At Newark Quality Roofing, we walk through each of these during a free on-site inspection so homeowners understand what is driving their specific number.
Roof Size, Pitch, and Height

Total surface area, not house square footage, determines how much roofing material and labor a project requires. A 2,000 square foot home often has 2,200 to 2,600 square feet of actual roof surface once pitch and overhangs are factored in (a pitch multiplier of 1.1 to 1.3). Many homeowners are surprised when their quote reflects more square footage than their floor plan.

Newark's housing stock includes row homes, two- and three-story colonials, multifamily buildings, and flat-roofed structures with parapets. Steeper roofs require specialized safety equipment and longer labor time; a roof with a 9/12 pitch takes 15% to 30% more labor hours than a walkable 4/12 pitch. Height matters, too: a three-story colonial requires more time to carry materials up and haul debris down, plus fall protection gear. Larger roofs benefit slightly from economies of scale (setup costs are spread over more squares), but the total cost still rises with area.
Roofing Material Selection

A typical asphalt shingle roof costs $6,000 to $9,000 to replace at the low end (basic 3-tab on a small, simple roof). Architectural asphalt shingles cost between $5,840 and $10,100 for replacement on average-sized homes. Metal roofing costs range from $10,245 to $41,640 for replacement, depending on the metal type, gauge, and panel style. The type of roofing material you choose shapes every other number on your quote, from installation costs to long-term maintenance. A detailed material-by-material price guide follows below.
Roof Complexity and Architectural Features

Roof complexity increases costs due to extra labor and materials. Complexity refers to the number of hips, valleys, dormers, skylights, chimneys, roof planes, and decorative trim. A simple gable roof with two planes and no penetrations is the cheapest to tear off and replace. A roof with six planes, two dormers, a skylight, and a chimney requires hours of additional cutting, fitting, and flashing work.

Complex roofs also generate more waste. Every hip, valley, and dormer means shingles and underlayment materials must be cut to fit, which increases the amount of material ordered (typically a 10% to 15% waste factor on a complex roof versus 5% on a simple gable). Many homes in Newark's older neighborhoods, particularly those built before 1940 in areas like Forest Hill and Weequahic, have intricate rooflines that push costs toward the upper end of local ranges.
Local Labor Rates, Permits, and Codes

Labor accounts for 40% to 60% of total roof replacement costs. In Essex County, labor rates exceed the national average; NJ roofing crews charge $68 to $110 per hour, which is one reason North Jersey quotes run higher than Sunbelt or Midwest numbers. Labor expenses vary based on geographic location, and Newark falls on the higher side of the national scale.

Permits for roof replacement typically cost between $100 and $500 at the municipal level, though some Newark projects see permit fees of $350 to $1,100 depending on the assessed project value; permits are filed with the City of Newark Building Division. New Jersey's Uniform Construction Code requires specific underlayment in eave areas, adequate roof ventilation, and wind uplift ratings that may require upgraded fastening patterns. These code requirements add both material and labor cost compared to states with less stringent building codes.
Existing Roof Condition and Number of Layers

The condition of your existing roof is the most common source of cost surprises. Removing multiple layers of old roofing increases labor and disposal costs; stripping two layers instead of one can add $1,500 to $3,000 to a typical project. Hidden structural damage discovered after tear-off adds repair costs that are impossible to quote before the old roof comes off.

A typical Newark scenario involves a 70- to 100-year-old home with at least two layers of old shingles and some rotted decking around the chimney or eaves. Rotted plywood decking costs $75 to $100 per 4x8 sheet to replace. If 10 to 15 sheets need replacement, that adds $750 to $1,500 to the project. Deteriorated rafters or fascia boards push costs higher still. This is why we recommend a contingency fund of 10% to 20% of the estimated total cost.

Asphalt Shingles (3-Tab and Architectural)

Three-tab asphalt shingles are the budget-friendly option, with total project costs for a mid-size Newark home running $8,000 to $13,000 installed, or roughly $3.00 to $5.00 per square foot. Architectural asphalt shingles cost $11,000 to $18,000 total, or about $5.50 to $8.50 per square foot.

Choosing asphalt shingles can save money on roof replacement compared to all other material types. They remain the most common roofing material in New Jersey for good reason: wide availability, fast installation, and strong manufacturer warranties. Newark Quality Roofing typically recommends architectural shingles over basic 3-tab because the cost difference per square foot is modest ($2 to $3 more) while the durability and wind resistance gains are measurable.
Premium Asphalt, Metal, and Designer Options

Premium asphalt shingles with impact ratings or designer profiles run $10 to $15 per square foot installed in North Jersey, putting total project cost at $18,000 to $30,000 for an average home. These products carry 30- to 50-year manufacturer warranties and may qualify for insurance premium discounts in areas prone to hail or wind.

The tradeoff is a 40- to 70-year lifespan, lower maintenance requirements, and energy efficiency from reflective coatings. On higher-value homes or properties where the owner plans to stay 20+ years, the higher cost per square foot can be offset by decades of avoided re-roofing.
Slate, Cedar, and Historic Roof Systems
Newark and nearby Essex County towns like Montclair and Glen Ridge have concentrations of historic homes originally roofed with natural slate or cedar.

Wooden shakes cost between $10,230 and $15,500 for replacement on an average home, with cedar shake running $8 to $14 per square foot installed. Synthetic slate products offer a middle ground: they mimic the appearance of natural slate at roughly half the installed cost while weighing far less, which avoids the structural reinforcement that natural slate's weight sometimes demands. Newark Quality Roofing evaluates the roof structure and framing capacity before recommending any heavy material like slate or concrete tile.
Flat and Low-Slope Roof Systems (TPO, EPDM, Modified Bitumen)

Flat and low-slope roofs are common on Newark row homes, small apartment buildings, and commercial properties. Tile roofing replacement costs between $10,665 and $20,900, but for truly flat roofs, membrane systems are required; shingles are not appropriate for slopes below 2/12.
(thermoplastic polyolefin) runs $6 to $12 per square foot installed and carries a 15- to 30-year lifespan depending on membrane thickness.

Modified bitumen falls in a similar range and is a common choice for Newark flat roofs because local contractors have decades of installation experience with the material. Flat roof tear-off costs tend to be lower per square foot than steep-slope tear-off because debris removal is simpler, but insulation replacement and edge detailing add costs that sloped roofs do not require.

runs.v: Tear-Off vs. Overlay: Why Skipping Tear-Off Often Costs More Later

An overlay saves roughly $1,500 to $4,000 on an average home by skipping tear-off and disposal. That savings comes at a cost: the old roof traps moisture against the deck, rotted decking goes undetected, and most manufacturer warranties are reduced or voided when new shingles are installed over old shingles. Newark and many Essex County municipalities limit roofs to two total layers. If your old roof already has two layers, a full tear-off is mandatory regardless of preference.

Newark Quality Roofing recommends full tear-off on nearly every project. The only scenario where we consider an overlay is a single-layer roof in confirmed good condition on a property being sold within a few years, where the owner understands the warranty limitations. Even then, code compliance and insurer requirements usually make a full tear-off the better choice.

sections.heading: Common Cost Surprises and How to Plan for Them

runs.v: Homeowners often budget for new shingles but overlook supporting components and hidden damage. A detailed contract should outline all costs and materials used; vague "roofing job" proposals are a red flag.
Hidden Decking and Structural Damage

Rotted decking, deteriorated rafters, and long-term leak damage are often invisible until the old roof comes off. Hidden structural damage discovered after tear-off adds repair costs that no contractor can predict from the ground. Common Newark scenarios include chronic chimney leaks that have softened surrounding sheathing, ice dam damage at eaves on north-facing slopes, and soft spots on older porch roofs.

Rotted plywood decking costs $75 to $100 per 4x8 sheet to replace. Fascia board replacement runs $8 to $15 per linear foot. On older homes where 10 to 20 sheets of decking and several feet of fascia need replacement, these structural repairs can add $1,000 to $3,000 to the project. A contingency fund of 10% to 20% of the estimated total helps cover these unexpected costs without delaying the project.
Flashing, Chimneys, Skylights, and Gutters
Replacing old step flashing, counter-flashing chimneys, re-sealing or replacing skylights, and installing

and downspouts all add to the final number. Chimney counter-flashing replacement typically costs $300 to $800. Skylight replacement or re-flashing runs $500 to $1,500 per unit. New seamless gutters cost $6 to $12 per linear foot installed.

Handling these upgrades during a roof replacement project is almost always cheaper than scheduling separate projects later, because scaffolding is already in place and the roof edge is accessible. Newark Quality Roofing inspects all these components during the estimate and flags anything that should be addressed while the roof is open.
Permits, Inspections, and Disposal Fees

Permits and inspections typically add $100 to $500 depending on the municipality. In Newark, some permit models run $350 to $1,100 for higher-value projects. Municipal inspectors may visit twice: once at the dry-in stage (underlayment complete) and once after final installation. Disposal fees depend on debris weight and local landfill rates; dumpster rental alone runs $300 to $600 for a typical residential tear-off.

Newark Quality Roofing pulls all required permits and includes permit fees in our quoted price. When comparing bids from different roofing contractors, confirm whether permits and disposal costs are included or listed separately; this is one of the most common reasons two quotes for the same roof look different.

The best way to manage the average cost to tear off and replace a roof is not to chase the lowest bid. It is to plan the project around your roof size, material preference, and the right time of year, then compare apples-to-apples estimates.
Setting a Realistic Roof Budget

Start with your roof's approximate square footage (not your home's floor area), then multiply by the per-square-foot range for your preferred material. Add 10% to 20% for contingency to cover rotted decking and underlayment repairs. If you want upgrades like impact-rated shingles, better ventilation, or new gutters, budget those as separate line items.

Newark Quality Roofing provides written estimates that break out each component. If your total cost exceeds your immediate budget, we can phase certain non-urgent upgrades (like gutter replacement) into a follow-up project while ensuring the core roof installation is complete and code-compliant.
Best Time of Year to Replace a Roof in North Jersey

Late spring through early fall is peak season for roofing projects in New Jersey. Crews are booked, scheduling lead times stretch to 4 to 6 weeks, and competitive pricing is harder to find. Fall offers stable weather and slightly shorter wait times. Schedule roof replacement in off-season for better pricing: late fall and early spring (November through March) can yield 5% to 10% savings and faster scheduling, though weather delays are possible and crew sizes may be smaller.
If you have active leaks or

Financing, Insurance, and Incentives

A new roof is a major investment. Common payment approaches include cash, home equity loans, personal loans, and contractor financing programs. Newark Quality Roofing can discuss available financing options during the estimate process.

Homeowners insurance may cover part of your roof replacement cost if the damage was caused by a covered event like wind, hail, or fallen trees. Normal wear and aging is not covered. If you have storm damage, document it promptly with photos, file a claim quickly, and request that your contractor provide a detailed scope of work to support the claim. New Jersey offers some energy efficiency incentives for cool roof coatings and solar-ready roofing systems. If you are planning a solar installation within the next few years, coordinating it with your roof replacement avoids the cost of removing and reinstalling panels later.

sections.heading: Choosing the Right Roofing Contractor in Newark, NJ

runs.v: A trustworthy, properly insured local roofer can protect your investment even if their bid is not the lowest number on the table. Cutting corners on contractor selection is the most expensive mistake homeowners make on roofing projects.
Comparing Estimates the Right Way

Get at least three detailed estimates from roofing contractors before committing. Each estimate should be based on an in-person inspection, not a phone quote or satellite measurement alone. Compare beyond the total price: check whether each bid specifies tear-off vs. overlay, names the shingle brand and product line, describes the underlayment type, and includes permits, flashing details, and cleanup.

Ask for line items or at least category-level breakdowns (materials vs. labor vs. permits). Two quotes that look $3,000 apart may actually be quoting different scopes. One may include ice and water shield at all valleys and eaves; the other may not. One may include rotted decking replacement allowance; the other may charge extra after tear-off. The cheapest quote is not always the most cost-effective quote.
Licensing, Insurance, and Warranties

Verify that contractors are licensed, bonded, and insured before signing anything. In New Jersey, roofing contractors must carry general liability insurance and workers' compensation coverage. Ask for certificates of insurance with current dates. Choose contractors with at least five years of experience; roofing failures from inexperienced installers often appear 2 to 5 years after installation, well after the crew has moved on.

Manufacturer warranties cover defects in the roofing material itself and typically run 25 to 50 years for architectural asphalt shingles. Workmanship warranties cover the installation and are issued by the contractor. runs.v: What is the average cost to tear off and replace a roof on a 1,500 sq ft home in Newark?

For a 1,500 square foot roof (actual roof surface, not floor area) with one existing layer of asphalt shingles, a simple gable shape, and architectural asphalt shingles as the replacement, expect $10,000 to $16,000 in 2026. That assumes moderate pitch, a one- or two-story home, and no major decking damage. Roof complexity, steep pitch, or premium materials push the number higher.
How long does a full tear-off and replacement usually take?

Most Newark single-family asphalt shingle jobs take 1 to 2 days from tear-off to final cleanup. Complex roofs with multiple dormers, steep pitch, or three stories may take 3 to 4 days. Slate, metal, or large multifamily projects can take a week or more depending on weather and material delivery schedules.
Is it ever okay to install new shingles over old ones to save money?

Installing new shingles over old shingles saves $1,500 to $4,000 but carries real downsides: hidden rot goes unrepaired, moisture can become trapped between layers, and most shingle manufacturer warranties are reduced or voided on overlay installations. New Jersey code limits roofs to two total layers. If your roof already has two layers, overlay is not an option. Newark Quality Roofing recommends full tear-off for nearly every residential project.
Can I replace just part of my roof to cut costs?

Partial replacement makes sense in limited situations: a recent addition with its own separate roof section, or clearly isolated damage from a fallen tree limb. On the rest of the roof, partial replacement creates color mismatch (even "matching" shingles from the same manufacturer will look different after a few years of weathering), uneven aging, and potential warranty gaps. For most roofs, replacing the entire roof at once is more cost effective over the life of the system.
How far in advance should I budget and schedule my roof replacement?

Plan 3 to 6 months before your desired installation window. This gives time to get at least three estimates, compare scopes, arrange financing if needed, and secure a spot on your contractor's schedule. If you need specific premium materials like natural slate or a particular metal panel, lead times for material delivery can add 4 to 8 weeks. Homeowners coordinating a roof with a solar installation or major renovation should start planning even earlier.
